title: Mira and the Library Flutter
markdown:
The oak doors of the town library were already swinging, and Mira the fox’s paws were twitchy before the first coat had been hung. Town Treasures evening had arrived two days sooner than her nerves had agreed to. In the museum archives she had coaxed a tarnished silver locket back toward gleam — not a prize, exactly, only a whisper of an honour: the little wooden spoon for Most Dedicated Preservationist. She wanted people to see the locket. She wanted the locket to be seen.

Bea the goat bleated from the armchair by the biography stacks, wool soft, enthusiasm boundless, a cushion corner already under consideration.

“It’ll be splendid, Mira. All the town’s treasures, right there. And your locket. Sparkle like a dewdrop on a spiderweb. Brighter than Mrs. Gable’s prize rhubarb, even.”

Mira managed a small smile. “Professor Gander is overseeing the programmes. You know how he is about order.”

She did know. Professor Gander, a goose of considerable gravitas, stood over a tower of programmes as if preparing a parade. Each bundle wore a precise crimson ribbon. His white feathers were starched into a kind of military peace. Wire-rimmed spectacles glinted in the library’s warm light.

“Now, now, Mira,” he huffed, parchment-dry. “These programmes must be presented with dignity. A town library is not a barn dance. Each recipient deserves an orderly, unruffled introduction to the evening’s treasures.”

Mira tried the locket with a soft cloth. It kept its storied dimness, as if shine would be a kind of forgetting. Bunting in slightly askew stripes of blue and yellow hung from the high shelves like cheerful fallen rainbows. Pottery shard, faded quill, the shy locket on purple velvet: she had placed each thing just so. The programmes, neat little soldiers, seemed to hum with a restlessness of their own, paper eager to be free.

Not a disaster yet: only the choice whether to polish the locket into a lie or let Gander’s empire of ribbon stand between the town and the table. Mira chose the cloth again, then set it down. The locket would whisper. She would greet people. She would not pick a fight with a goose about bows.

Townspeople trickled in. Mira’s greetings were tentative, her gaze darting between velvet and fortress. Then a poorly latched window near History admitted a small, mischievous gust. It caught the top bundle. Ribbons snapped. Programmes pirouetted through the hall like an unexpected blizzard.

“Oh dear,” Mira said, and her heart went into her throat. Order, dissolving.

“Disarray!” Professor Gander’s beak fell open. “Utter disarray!” His feathers ruffled as if gravity had become a personal insult.

Bea landed among the scattering sheets with surprising grace. Her hooves, usually gifted at clover, nudged paper into nascent piles.

“Don’t worry, Professor! We are not losing control. We are broadening the interpretation. A joyful distribution!” Perhaps, she added, the programmes simply wanted to explore more of the library.

Mira could have frozen. She could have run for the window and the ribbons and the cloth. She looked at Gander’s alarm, at Bea’s sunbeam cheer, and chose the floor. A young boy chased a loop-the-loop near the ceiling. A woman with a basket of yarn gathered a fallen stack as smoothly as knitting. Mrs. Higgins, who usually spoke only of prize begonias, re-tied ribbons with fierce maternal concentration. Mira found herself among children, sorting programmes into colourful, mixed-up heaps. They giggled. The stern red ribbons made friends with cheerful paper. Even Gander’s starched feathers seemed, slightly, to forgive the air.

He watched the collaborative chaos. His stern expression softened into thought. He adjusted his spectacles. A tiny smile visited his beak.

“Perhaps,” he murmured, “a rather efficient redistribution. A dynamic presentation. It certainly adds a flutter to the proceedings.”

By the time Town Treasures truly began, the library hummed. Programmes — some neatly tied by determined hands, others artfully clustered — went out as shared work. Mira’s locket, no longer bullied into unnatural sheen, sat not on a solitary cushion but on a table among other charming objects, each with a tale. Conversations flowed. Laughter found the rafters. Professor Gander, surprisingly happy, directed people toward the refreshments.

He gave Mira not the whispered wooden spoon but a cheerful, approving nod. Bea offered a woolly hug and admired the jumbled stacks as if they were a garden that had decided to bloom out of season.

Mira looked around the bustling room. The locket, nestled among shared stories, held a light that had nothing to do with polish. She left the cloth in her pocket, and did not take it out again.
characters: Mira (museum-conservator fox), Bea (goat flatmate), Gander (starched library goose)
